claims.claim: The five gene clusters most highly upregulated in S. venezuelae explorer cells encode the ATP synthase complex, two predicted cation/proton antiporter complexes, and two peptide transporters.
claims.source: The five gene clusters mostly highly upregulated in S. venezuelae explorer cells encoded the ATP synthase complex (sven_5018-26; 7.6-fold increase relative to non-spreading), two predicted cation/proton antiporter complexes (95.9- and 85.3-fold increase relative to non-spreading for sven_5668-72 and sven_5764-68, respectively), and two peptide transporters (17.4- and 38.3-fold increase relative to non-spreading for sven_4759-63 and sven_5150-54, respectively) (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Higher expression of cation/proton antiporters and increased ATP synthesis would be expected to enhance proton uptake into the cell.
claims.source: Higher expression of the cation/proton antiporters, alongside increased ATP synthesis, would be expected to enhance proton uptake into the cell; equivalent genes are upregulated as part of the alkaline stress response in other bacteria (Krulwich et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data and supported by citation to Krulwich et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Amino acid catabolism is upregulated under alkaline growth conditions in other bacteria.
claims.source: Amino acid catabolism is also upregulated under alkaline growth conditions in other bacteria (Padan et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Padan et al., 2005.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae exploratory growth requires an amino acid source.
claims.source: Given the dramatically increased expression of the peptide transporters, we confirmed that exploratory growth required an amino acid source (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is confirmed by experimental testing mentioned in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae exploration is coupled with a metabolic reprogramming that permits robust growth under highly alkaline conditions.
claims.source: Collectively, these results suggest that exploration is coupled with a metabolic reprogramming that permits robust growth under highly alkaline conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq and mutant data.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae explorer cells produced a basic VOC that raised the pH of physically separated medium from 7.0 to 9.5.
claims.source: After 10 days, we measured the pH of the uninoculated YPD compartment, and found the compartment adjacent to S. venezuelae alone remained at pH 7.0, whereas the one adjacent to S. venezuelae explorer cells had risen from pH 7.0 to 9.5, indicating the explorer cells produced a basic VOC (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the two-compartment assay shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae growing alone on glucose-deficient agar could alkalinize adjacent YPD medium.
claims.source: To verify that the VOC was produced by S. venezuelae explorers and not by S. cerevisiae, we repeated the two-compartment assay with S. venezuelae grown alone on G- agar, a condition that also induced exploratory behaviour. We found that S. venezuelae growing alone on G- agar could alkalinize the adjacent YPD compartment. This confirmed that a basic VOC was produced by S. venezuelae explorer cells (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the two-compartment assay shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae explorer cells released a VOC that promoted exploratory growth in distantly located S. venezuelae cells.
claims.source: As expected, after 10 days, the S. cerevisiae-associated cells were actively spreading. Remarkably, the adjacent S. venezuelae cells (in the absence of yeast) had also initiated exploratory growth (Figure 4C). As a negative control, S. venezuelae alone was grown in both compartments on YPD agar; spreading was not observed for cells grown in either compartment after 10 days (Figure 4C). These data implied that S. venezuelae explorer cells released a VOC that effectively promoted exploratory growth in distantly located S. venezuelae cells.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the two-compartment assay shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The S. venezuelae cydCD mutant was capable of exploration when stimulated by neighboring explorer cells.
claims.source: We tested whether our exploration-deficient cydCD mutant was able to respond to this VOC, and observed that despite its inability to explore when grown next to yeast, this mutant was capable of exploration when stimulated by neighbouring explorer cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae explorers can stimulate exploratory growth of the wild Streptomyces isolate WAC0566 through VOC signaling.
claims.source: After 10 days, WAC0566 grown adjacent to S. venezuelae explorers initiated exploratory growth, and this was not seen for the negative control (Figure 4D). This indicated that exploratory growth could be communicated to unrelated streptomycetes.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the two-compartment assay shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Exploratory growth can be communicated to unrelated streptomycetes.
claims.source: This indicated that exploratory growth could be communicated to unrelated streptomycetes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inter-species VOC communication experiments.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae exploration can be stimulated by a VOC produced by yeast-associated WAC0566.
claims.source: We tested the volatile-mediated communication between these strains in a reciprocal experiment, and found that S. venezuelae exploration could also be stimulated by a VOC produced by yeast-associated WAC0566 (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the reciprocal two-compartment assay shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: VOC communication of exploratory growth was observed for at least 13 wild Streptomyces strains.
claims.source: This inter-species promotion of S. venezuelae exploration was observed for at least 13 other wild Streptomyces strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: VOC communication of exploratory growth was confined to species with exploratory capabilities.
claims.source: Importantly, VOC communication of exploratory growth was confined to those species with exploratory capabilities (S. coelicolor failed to respond to the VOC elicitor).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from testing S. coelicolor response to the VOC.

claims.claim: The exploration-promoting VOC can be produced by liquid-grown glucose-deficient cultures.
claims.source: We determined that the exploration-promoting VOC could be produced by liquid-grown (G-) cultures, and that it stimulated exploratory growth by both S. venezuelae and WAC0566 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: VOC production is glucose-repressible.
claims.source: To rule out the possibility that any liquid-grown culture could promote exploration, we also grew S. venezuelae and WAC0566 in YPD (G+) liquid medium, and found these cultures were unable to stimulate exploration. This suggested that VOC production was glucose-repressible, and its production correlated with growth conditions that promoted exploration.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing G+ and G- liquid culture experiments.

claims.claim: 1400 unique compounds were identified from S. venezuelae and WAC0566 culture supernatants using GC×GC-TOFMS.
claims.source: We collected the supernatants of each culture, and assayed them using two-dimensional gas chromatography time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC×GC-TOFMS). From this, 1400 unique compounds were identified.
claims.evidence: This is a result from GC×GC-TOFMS analysis.

claims.claim: Four compounds were detected in 100% of S. venezuelae and WAC0566 exploration-promoting cultures: trimethylamine (TMA), thiocyanic acid, 6-methyl-5-hepten-2-one, and 2-acetylthiazole.
claims.source: Within this group of 12, only four were detected in 100% of S. venezuelae and WAC0566 exploration-promoting cultures: trimethylamine (TMA), thiocyanic acid, 6-methyl-5-hepten-2-one, and 2-acetylthiazole.
claims.evidence: This is a result from filtering the GC×GC-TOFMS data.

claims.claim: TMA was >10 fold more abundant than the other three candidate compounds.
claims.source: Notably, TMA was >10 fold more abundant than the other three compounds, and thus we focussed our initial investigations on this molecule.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the GC×GC-TOFMS data.

claims.claim: TMA is a volatile nitrogen-containing metabolite with a high pKa (9.81).
claims.source: TMA is a volatile nitrogen-containing metabolite with a high pKa (9.81).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known chemical property of TMA.

claims.claim: TMA was responsible for promoting S. venezuelae exploration.
claims.source: After seven days, S. venezuelae cultured adjacent to the TMA-emitting solutions had initiated exploratory growth, while those grown next to a water-containing control failed to spread. This implied that TMA was the VOC used by S. venezuelae and WAC0566 to elicit exploratory growth.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the TMA exposure experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae lacks any gene with similarity to cntA.
claims.source: S. venezuelae lacks any gene with similarity to cntA, and thus does not use an equivalent pathway to generate TMA.
claims.evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the S. venezuelae genome.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae cutCD homologues were more highly expressed in static cultures than in spreading cultures.
claims.source: It does possess homologues of cutCD; however, these genes were more highly expressed (~5 fold) in static S. venezuelae cultures (where no TMA was ever detected), than in spreading cultures.
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data comparing static and explorer cells.

claims.claim: TMA raised the pH of non-inoculated YPD agar from 7.0 to 9.5.
claims.source: To confirm that TMA could raise the pH of the growth medium in the same way as explorer cells, we measured the pH of non-inoculated YPD agar around dishes containing TMA, and found the pH rose from 7.0 to 9.5.
claims.evidence: This is a measurement from pH assays with TMA.

claims.claim: TMA failed to induce S. venezuelae exploration to the same extent on buffered plates (pH 7.0) as on non-buffered plates.
claims.source: To test whether TMA induced exploratory growth by raising the pH, we repeated our plate assays described in Figure 4E, and buffered the agar to 7.0 using 50 or 200 mM MOPS (Figure 4F). The pH of these plates rose to 8.0 (as opposed to 9.5 on non-buffered plates), and TMA failed to induce S. venezuelae exploration to the same extent as on non-buffered plates.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the buffering experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Ammonia induced S. venezuelae exploratory growth after seven days.
claims.source: To further validate the pH-mediated effect of TMA, we tested whether ammonia (another basic VOC) had the same effect (Figure 4E). After seven days, ammonia induced S. venezuelae exploratory growth, suggesting that VOC-mediated alkalinity stimulated Streptomyces exploration.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the ammonia exposure experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: VOC-mediated alkalinity stimulates Streptomyces exploration.
claims.source: After seven days, ammonia induced S. venezuelae exploratory growth, suggesting that VOC-mediated alkalinity stimulated Streptomyces exploration.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ammonia and TMA experiments.

claims.claim: B. subtilis and M. luteus colony numbers were reduced by an average of 17.4% and 25.1%, respectively, on plates exposed to VOCs produced by exploratory S. venezuelae.
claims.source: B. subtilis and M. luteus colony numbers were reduced by an average of 17.4% and 25.1%, respectively, on plates exposed to VOCs produced by exploratory S. venezuelae, relative to those grown adjacent to static cultures.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from bacterial survival assays shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: An approximately 50% drop in viable B. subtilis and M. luteus cells was observed when exposed to 0.9% TMA.
claims.source: We observed an approximately 50% drop in viable cells when exposed to 0.9% TMA, and in the case of B. subtilis, a further drop in viability was observed as TMA concentrations increased.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from TMA exposure experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: TMA adversely affects the growth and survival of other soil bacteria.
claims.source: This confirmed that TMA adversely affected the growth and survival of other soil bacteria.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TMA exposure experiments on B. subtilis and M. luteus.

claims.claim: Exploratory growth represents a powerful new addition to the Streptomyces developmental repertoire.
claims.source: Exploratory growth represents a powerful new addition to the Streptomyces developmental repertoire, and one that appears to be well-integrated into the existing life cycle.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claims.claim: When grown next to yeast, S. venezuelae explorer cells emerge from a mass of sporulating cells.
claims.source: When grown next to yeast, explorer cells emerge from a mass of sporulating cells (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental observations shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The functional differentiation of explorer and sporulating cells represents an effective bet-hedging strategy.
claims.source: This functional differentiation represents an effective bet-hedging strategy, whereby spreading explorer cells scavenge nutrients for the group, while the sporulating cells provide a highly resistant genetic repository, ensuring colony survival in the event of failed exploration.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the biological significance of the observed differentiation.

claims.claim: S. venezuelae explorer cells dispense with frequent branching as a trade-off for the ability to rapidly spread to new environments.
claims.source: We presume that explorer cells dispense with frequent branching as a trade-off for the ability to rapidly spread to new environments.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the non-branching morphology.

claims.claim: Exploratory growth occurs independently of the typical bld- and whi-developmental determinants.
claims.source: Exploratory growth also occurs independently of the typical bld- and whi-developmental determinants, supporting the notion that this is a unique growth strategy.
claims.evidence: This is based on the mutant analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: BldN regulon members may help to facilitate the exploration process.
claims.source: It is possible, however, given the slower exploration observed for bldN mutants (where bldN encodes a sigma factor), that BldN regulon members help to facilitate the exploration process.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the bldN mutant phenotype.

claims.claim: Exploratory growth capability may be more broadly conserved in Streptomyces than observed in this study.
claims.source: While we observed exploratory growth in a subset of Streptomyces species, it is possible that this capability is more broadly conserved and is stimulated by different conditions than those investigated here.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential broader distribution of exploratory growth.

claims.claim: Interactions between different organisms within soil microbial communities are likely to be more the norm than the exception.
claims.source: Indeed, microbes are abundant in the soil, and interactions between different organisms within these communities are likely to be more the norm than the exception.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about microbial ecology in soil.

claims.claim: Inter-species interactions are important in bacterial development as a key to revealing novel growth strategies.
claims.source: Our work illustrates the importance of inter-species interactions in bacterial development, as a key to revealing novel growth strategies.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claims.claim: Long-range communication strategies in the form of volatile compounds may play widespread roles in regulating development and metabolic activities in microbial communities.
claims.source: It also emphasises the need to consider long-range communication strategies, in the form of volatile compounds, which may play widespread roles in regulating development and metabolic activities in microbial communities.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the VOC signaling findings.

results.result: Interactions between S. venezuelae and S. cerevisiae trigger a novel mode of bacterial development termed 'exploratory growth', characterized by non-branching, hydrophilic cells that rapidly traverse solid surfaces at rates (~1.5 µm/min) an order of magnitude faster than growth alone. This behavior is distinct from the canonical Streptomyces life cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C29-C34, C36-C38, and C43 collectively demonstrate the discovery of exploratory growth through multiple lines of evidence: time-lapse microscopy (C33-C34), SEM imaging (C36-C37), hydrophilicity assays (C38), and barrier-crossing experiments (C32). The morphological and kinetic characterization is well-documented, and the distinction from canonical development is supported by mutant analysis (C43).

results.result: Exploratory growth occurs independently of the typical bld and whi developmental determinants, with all tested mutants displaying exploratory behavior similar to wild type after 14 days, though the bldN mutant exhibited slower exploration.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 and C113 are supported by systematic testing of developmental mutants shown in Figure 1D. The observation that bld and whi mutants retain exploratory capacity while showing expected defects in aerial hyphae formation and sporulation (C41-C42) provides strong evidence that exploration is genetically distinct from canonical development. The slower exploration of bldN mutants (C40, C114) is noted but does not contradict the main conclusion.

results.result: Approximately 10% of 200 wild Streptomyces isolates exhibited exploratory growth, and phylogenetic analysis revealed that explorer-competent strains do not form a monophyletic group, suggesting exploratory growth is widespread in the streptomycetes.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by systematic screening data (C45) and phylogenetic analysis (C46, Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The quantitative result (19/200 strains, ~10%) is clearly stated, and the phylogenetic distribution supports the inference that exploratory growth is widespread rather than confined to a single lineage. The negative results for well-studied species (C44) provide appropriate controls.

results.result: A broad range of microbial fungi can trigger S. venezuelae exploratory growth, with all tested species except C. neoformans and P. fermentans inducing the behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by systematic testing of multiple fungal species shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3. The breadth of fungi tested (8 species from diverse genera) and the high success rate (6/8) support the conclusion that exploratory growth can be triggered by a broad range of fungi. The two exceptions (C. neoformans and P. fermentans) are appropriately noted.

results.result: Screening of S. cerevisiae knockout mutants identified 16 strains unable to promote exploration, with 13 affecting mitochondrial function including 8 in TCA cycle genes, suggesting that fungal respiration and TCA cycle function influence exploratory growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 and C55 are supported by systematic screening of 4309 S. cerevisiae mutants with clear quantitative results (16 mutants identified, 13 affecting mitochondrial function, 8 in TCA cycle). The functional enrichment for mitochondrial/TCA cycle genes is striking and supports the mechanistic inference (C55). Confirmation in C. albicans mutants (mentioned in text) provides additional validation.

results.result: Glucose represses S. venezuelae exploratory growth. S. cerevisiae consumed glucose during growth (3.8-fold reduction), and growth on glucose-deficient medium permitted exploration regardless of yeast presence.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 and C67 are supported by glucose measurements (C56-C57, Figure 2B) and growth experiments on glucose-deficient medium (C58, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The glucose depletion by yeast is quantified, and the ability of S. venezuelae to explore on G- medium without yeast provides strong evidence for glucose repression. This is a key mechanistic finding.

results.result: TCA cycle mutants (ΔLPD1, ΔKGD2) that fail to promote exploration consumed similar glucose levels as wild type but lowered agar pH to 5.5 (vs. 7.5 for wild type). Buffering to pH 7.0 restored exploration-promoting ability, and supplementing medium with citrate or acetate inhibited exploration, confirming that secreted acids inhibit exploratory growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 are supported by glucose measurements (C60, Figure 2B), pH measurements (C62-C63, Figure 2B), buffering experiments (C64, Figure 2C), and acid supplementation experiments (C65, Figure 2D). The logic is sound: TCA cycle mutants blocked after citrate production accumulate and secrete organic acids, lowering pH and inhibiting exploration. Buffering rescues the phenotype, confirming pH-dependence.

results.result: S. venezuelae exploration is associated with a rise in pH from 7.0 to 9.5, mediated by Streptomyces cells. However, high pH alone is not sufficient to promote exploration, suggesting an adaptation phase is required during the transition to exploratory growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C73 are supported by pH measurements during exploration (C68-C69, Figure 3A), pH rise in absence of yeast (C70, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and failure to induce exploration on pH 9.0 buffered medium (C71, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The conclusion that alkaline conditions are necessary but not sufficient (C72) is well-supported, and the inference of an adaptation requirement (C73) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Three exploration-defective mutants harbored point mutations in the sven_3713-3716 operon encoding the cytochrome bd oxidase complex and an ABC transporter for cytochrome assembly. Complementation experiments confirmed that the cytochrome bd oxidase complex is essential for S. venezuelae exploration.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by whole genome sequencing (C74), bioinformatic prediction (C75), and complementation experiments (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3). The genetic evidence is strong: independent mutants map to the same operon, and complementation restores the phenotype. The essentiality of cytochrome bd oxidase for exploration is well-established.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis revealed that explorer cells highly upregulate genes encoding ATP synthase, cation/proton antiporters (95.9- and 85.3-fold), and peptide transporters (17.4- and 38.3-fold), consistent with an alkaline stress response. Exploratory growth requires an amino acid source and is coupled with metabolic reprogramming for growth under highly alkaline conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 are supported by RNA-seq data (C79, Figure 3D) showing dramatic upregulation of alkaline stress-responsive genes. The fold-changes are quantified and substantial. The interpretation (C80, C83) is supported by citations to alkaline stress responses in other bacteria (C78, C80, C81). The requirement for amino acids (C82) is confirmed experimentally. The cytochrome bd oxidase function (C77) is established knowledge.

results.result: S. venezuelae explorer cells produce a basic VOC that raises the pH of physically separated medium from 7.0 to 9.5. This was confirmed using two-compartment assays with explorer cells grown beside yeast or alone on glucose-deficient medium.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by two-compartment assays (Figure 4A-B) showing pH rise in physically separated medium. The experimental design with appropriate controls (S. venezuelae alone on G+ medium showing no pH rise) is sound. The conclusion that explorer cells produce a basic VOC is well-supported.

results.result: S. venezuelae explorer cells release a VOC that promotes exploratory growth in distantly located S. venezuelae cells. The exploration-deficient cydCD mutant, unable to explore when grown next to yeast, was capable of exploration when stimulated by neighboring explorer cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by two-compartment assays (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) with appropriate negative controls. The ability of the cydCD mutant to respond to the VOC (C87) is particularly important, demonstrating that the VOC acts downstream of or independently from the cytochrome bd oxidase requirement for VOC production.

results.result: Exploratory growth can be communicated between unrelated Streptomyces species via VOC signaling. S. venezuelae explorers stimulated exploration in wild isolate WAC0566, and reciprocally, yeast-associated WAC0566 stimulated S. venezuelae exploration. This inter-species communication was observed for at least 13 wild strains and was confined to species with exploratory capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 are supported by systematic two-compartment assays (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) demonstrating bidirectional inter-species communication. The observation that 13 additional wild strains show this behavior (C91) and that S. coelicolor (non-explorer) fails to respond (C92) provides strong evidence for specificity. The conclusion of inter-species communication (C89) is well-supported.

results.result: The exploration-promoting VOC can be produced by liquid-grown glucose-deficient cultures but not by glucose-containing cultures, indicating that VOC production is glucose-repressible and correlates with growth conditions that promote exploration.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by liquid culture experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) showing that G- but not G+ liquid cultures can stimulate exploration. This is consistent with the glucose repression of exploration observed on solid medium and supports the mechanistic model. The experimental design with appropriate controls is sound.

results.result: GC×GC-TOFMS analysis identified 1400 compounds, with four detected in 100% of exploration-promoting cultures: TMA, thiocyanic acid, 6-methyl-5-hepten-2-one, and 2-acetylthiazole. TMA was >10-fold more abundant and has a high pKa (9.81). Exposure to TMA solutions induced S. venezuelae exploratory growth, identifying TMA as the exploration-promoting VOC.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 are supported by systematic GC×GC-TOFMS analysis with stringent filtering criteria and functional validation (Figure 4E). The identification of TMA as the key VOC is well-supported by its abundance (C97), chemical properties (C98), and functional testing (C99). The experimental approach is rigorous and the conclusion is sound.

results.result: S. venezuelae lacks genes similar to cntA and possesses cutCD homologues that were more highly expressed (~5-fold) in static cultures where no TMA was detected, suggesting these genes do not direct TMA production in S. venezuelae.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 are supported by bioinformatic analysis (C100) and RNA-seq data (C101). The negative correlation between cutCD expression and TMA production argues against their involvement in TMA synthesis. However, the mechanism of TMA production remains unclear, which is acknowledged in the text. This is appropriate scientific reasoning from negative evidence.

results.result: TMA raises the pH of non-inoculated medium from 7.0 to 9.5. Buffering to pH 7.0 reduced TMA-induced exploration, and ammonia (another basic VOC) also induced exploration, demonstrating that VOC-mediated alkalinity stimulates Streptomyces exploration.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 are supported by pH measurements (C102), buffering experiments (C103, Figure 4F), and ammonia exposure experiments (C104, Figure 4E). The logic is sound: TMA's ability to induce exploration is pH-dependent, and another basic VOC (ammonia) has the same effect, supporting the conclusion that alkalinity is the key mechanism (C105).

results.result: VOCs produced by exploratory S. venezuelae reduced B. subtilis and M. luteus colony numbers by 17.4% and 25.1%, respectively. Direct TMA exposure (0.9%) caused ~50% reduction in viable cells, confirming that TMA adversely affects the growth and survival of other soil bacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 are supported by bacterial survival assays (Figure 5B-C) with appropriate controls and quantification. The effects are statistically significant (indicated by asterisks in Figure 5B-C) and dose-dependent for B. subtilis (C107). The conclusion that TMA has antibacterial activity (C108) is well-supported.

results.result: Exploratory growth represents a powerful addition to the Streptomyces developmental repertoire. When grown next to yeast, explorer cells emerge from a mass of sporulating cells, representing a bet-hedging strategy where explorers scavenge nutrients while sporulating cells provide a genetic repository.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by experimental observations (C110, Figure 6) showing coexistence of explorer and sporulating cells. The interpretation as a bet-hedging strategy (C111) is reasonable given the functional differentiation observed. However, C111 is partly interpretive (INFERENCE evidence type), and the bet-hedging hypothesis, while plausible, is not directly tested.

results.result: This work demonstrates that interkingdom interactions can trigger novel developmental behaviors in bacteria, and that VOCs can act as long-range communication signals capable of propagating microbial morphological switches, emphasizing the importance of inter-species interactions and volatile compounds in regulating development in microbial communities.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C117-C118 represent the major conclusions of the study, synthesizing findings from exploratory growth discovery, VOC-mediated communication, and inter-species signaling. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence presented throughout the manuscript. The claims are appropriately framed as broader implications of the specific findings.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on the canonical Streptomyces life cycle, including spore germination, vegetative hyphal growth, aerial hyphae formation, and sporulation, along with the roles of bld and whi genes, and notes that all characterized Streptomyces cell types are non-motile.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C14-C28 represent established knowledge about Streptomyces biology, supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims provide necessary context for understanding the novelty of exploratory growth. The evidence types are primarily KNOWLEDGE and CITATION, which is appropriate for background information.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on polymicrobial communities and interspecies interactions, noting that most bacteria and fungi exist in larger communities where interactions can modify virulence, antibiotic resistance, growth, and metabolite production, and that such interactions are likely common in soil.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C13 and C116 represent established knowledge about microbial ecology and interspecies interactions, supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide context for the significance of the fungal-bacterial interaction studied. The evidence is primarily from CITATION, which is appropriate for background information.

results.result: The authors speculate that explorer cells dispense with branching as a trade-off for rapid spreading, that BldN regulon members may facilitate exploration, and that exploratory growth capability may be more broadly conserved in Streptomyces than observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C114, and C115 are explicitly speculative (evidence type SPECULATION) and represent hypotheses for future investigation rather than conclusions supported by the current data. C112 is a reasonable interpretation of the non-branching morphology, C114 is based on the slower exploration of bldN mutants, and C115 acknowledges limitations of the current screen. These are appropriately framed as speculation in the Discussion.
